title: Stream Cipher
body:
A [[Symmetric Key Cryptography|symmetric]] cipher that encrypts one bit or byte at a time by
**XOR-ing the plaintext with a keystream**:

$$c_i = m_i \oplus z_i, \qquad m_i = c_i \oplus z_i$$

Encryption and decryption are the *same operation*, because XOR is its own inverse. In the language
of [[ABSTRACT ALGEBRA]] that is characteristic 2: in $GF(2)$, $x + x = 0$, so addition and
subtraction coincide. See [[Finite Field]].

The whole design problem is generating $z$. The key is short and the message is long, so a
deterministic generator stretches a short seed into a long keystream, which makes a stream cipher a
cryptographically strong [[Random Numbers|pseudo-random number generator]] wearing a different hat.

## The one-time pad, and why it is not the answer

If $z$ is **truly random, as long as the message, and never reused**, the cipher is *information
theoretically secure*: given $c$, every plaintext of that length is equally likely, so the
ciphertext carries no information about the message at all. Shannon proved it, and it is the only
scheme in the course with a security proof that does not rest on a hardness assumption.

It is also unusable. The key is as long as the message, so distributing it is exactly as hard as
distributing the message securely in the first place. A stream cipher is the engineering
compromise: **replace "truly random" with "computationally indistinguishable from random", and buy
back the short key.** Everything that can go wrong follows from that swap.

## Never reuse a keystream

The cardinal rule, and the one people break. Encrypt two messages under the same keystream and the
XOR cancels it:

$$c_1 \oplus c_2 = (m_1 \oplus z) \oplus (m_2 \oplus z) = m_1 \oplus m_2$$

The attacker now has the XOR of two plaintexts and no key involved. Both fall to
[[Cryptanalysis|frequency analysis]] on the combined stream, because English XOR English is not
uniform. This is why stream ciphers take a **nonce** alongside the key: the key is reused across
sessions, the nonce never is, and the keystream is a function of both.

## LFSRs

The classic hardware keystream generator, and the point where a 4th-year MATH course lands
directly on a 2nd-year hardware note. A **linear feedback shift register** is a
[[Shift Register]] whose input bit is the XOR of a fixed set of its own cells (the *taps*):

```
taps at positions 4 and 1        feedback = b4 XOR b1
    +---+---+---+---+
--> | b4| b3| b2| b1| --> output bit
    +---+---+---+---+
      ^                 |
      +----- XOR <------+

state 1001 -> 1100 -> 0110 -> 1011 -> ...
```

Everything about it is [[Boolean Algebra]] over $GF(2)$:

- The state update is a **linear map**, a matrix over $GF(2)$ applied to the state vector. That is
  [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]] with a two-element field of scalars.
- An $n$-bit register has $2^n - 1$ non-zero states, and if the tap polynomial is
  [[Irreducibility|irreducible]] and primitive the register cycles through **all** of them before
  repeating: a maximal-length sequence, $m$-sequence, of period $2^n - 1$. The generator of the
  [[Cyclic Group]] of non-zero elements of $GF(2^n)$ is what that period is counting.
- The all-zero state is a fixed point and is excluded, which is why the period is $2^n-1$ and not
  $2^n$.

**An LFSR alone is not a cipher.** It is linear, so $2n$ known keystream bits determine the taps and
the state by solving a linear system (the Berlekamp-Massey algorithm does it efficiently), and the
rest of the keystream falls out. Real LFSR-based ciphers combine several registers through a
non-linear function, clock them irregularly, or both. The lesson is the one from
[[Symmetric Key Cryptography]]: **linear is breakable, and non-linearity has to be added on
purpose.**

RC4 (software, byte-oriented, now broken and removed from TLS) and ChaCha20 (the current default)
are the practical successors. They keep the XOR-with-keystream shape and replace the linear
generator with something that resists the algebraic attack.
